title: First World War poets: Owen, Sassoon and the pity of war
examples: What does Dulce et decorum est mean?
How did Owen and Sassoon meet?
How is Owen different from Rupert Brooke?

explain.say: In 1914 young men queued to join up, and Rupert Brooke wrote that if he died, some corner of a foreign field would be for ever England. Four years later Wilfred Owen wrote that his subject was war, and the pity of war. The board compares these two voices. A gentle note: this poetry describes death in battle plainly.

draw.text: First World War poets: Owen, Sassoon and the pity of war

explain.say: Follow Owen's poem Dulce et Decorum Est. Exhausted men trudge back from the line; someone shouts gas; one soldier is too slow with his mask and dies as the poet watches through the green haze. Owen ends by calling the old Latin motto, that it is sweet to die for your country, the old Lie. Who do you think he is speaking to?

explain.say: Look at the timeline. In 1917 Sassoon, a decorated officer, publicly protested that the war was being needlessly prolonged. Instead of a court martial he was sent to Craiglockhart, an Edinburgh hospital for shell-shocked officers, where he met a shy young poet: Owen. Sassoon read his drafts and urged him on. What changes when a poet finds a mentor?

explain.say: Now sort their tools. Owen uses pararhyme, near-rhymes with the same consonants but different vowels, which sound unsettled, as if something has gone wrong. Sassoon prefers sharp satire: short poems with a bitter punchline aimed at generals and cheering crowds at home. Brooke writes polished sonnets of glory. Which tool hits hardest for you?

The map shows the journey. Owen recovered in Edinburgh, then chose to return to the front in France to speak for his men. He was killed on 4 November 1918, one week before the Armistice; his mother's telegram arrived as church bells rang for peace. Thank you for listening so carefully. Challenge: read Anthem for Doomed Youth and find the sounds of the guns.

draw.label: Owen recovered at Craiglockhart in Edinburgh, then returned to the Western Front in France

faq.q: What does Dulce et decorum est mean?
faq.a: It is Latin from the Roman poet Horace: it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country. Owen quotes it at the end of his gas-attack poem and calls it the old Lie.
asks: Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori meaning

faq.q: How did Owen and Sassoon meet?
faq.a: At Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh in August 1917, where both were being treated. Owen, a great admirer, showed Sassoon his drafts, and Sassoon encouraged him to write plainly about the war.

faq.q: How is Owen different from Rupert Brooke?
faq.a: Brooke, writing in 1914 before he saw the trenches, presents death as a noble gift to England. Owen, writing from the front in 1917 and 1918, shows gas, mud and suffering and focuses on pity.

In July 1917 Sassoon issued a statement, read out in Parliament, saying the war was being deliberately prolonged by those who could end it. The army sent him to Craiglockhart rather than court-martial a decorated hero.
A half-rhyme in which the consonants match but the vowels differ, such as hall and hell. Owen used it to create a sense of unease and incompleteness.

facts: Wilfred Owen was killed on 4 November 1918, aged 25, at the Sambre–Oise Canal in France.
Only five of Owen's poems were published in his lifetime; Sassoon helped bring out a collection in 1920.
Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori comes from the Odes of the Roman poet Horace.
